{"body": "Three responses now sit on the table, and they are not three answers to one question. The account proposes a specification remedy. The objection attacks the ordering and the discriminating power of the account's test. The rival shifts the axis from "what did we agree to" to "what is this flat." Here is what I would keep, change, and leave alone.

**The objection's strongest point.** Its o2 lands. The account floats a test — try two or three concrete items and see whether recurrence falls — and then treats falling recurrence as support for the ambiguity reading (c2). It is not that. Falling recurrence is compatible with ambiguity, with load imbalance (clearer paperwork can lower friction on a lopsided arrangement without making it less lopsided), with renegotiation-after-schedule-change, and with the rival's household-kind reading; recurrence can also migrate into new complaint items or return after the next schedule change. The test has low discriminating power, not zero. The account's c2 should be revised where it says falling recurrence supports c1 and rising recurrence weakens it.

But the objection's own o4 is honest and matters: if the flatmates genuinely cannot say what they agreed to, ambiguity is the plainest reading and the alternatives are harder to reach from the material. My position: ambiguity is the most parsimonious reading of the one reported fact ("later disagree about what the agreement meant"), and parsimony is a reason to start there, not a reason to call the test confirmatory.

The objection's phrasing complaint — that "thin" is the author's characterization — is technically true and does less work than it wants. "Thin" is a caveat about what may be asserted, and the account does keep its claims hedged. The fault is ordering, not vocabulary; o3 says as much. I would accept the ordering complaint and drop the vocabulary one.

**What the rival adds.** r2 is a genuinely different axis, not a fourth competitor on the same question. If the disputes are partly about whether the flat is a unit with obligations or three private lives sharing fixtures, then tightened specifications are not neutral clarification; they enact one side. That conditional is real: r3 follows from r2. But r2 is admitted to be a conjecture resting on a single withdrawal, so I hold r3 conditional rather than adopted. If r2 is true, the rival is right that a plan addressing only ambiguity keeps hitting a wall.

The rival's r7 is the most discriminating cheap observation in the whole set: watch whether the withdrawing flatmate engages with the *content* of a proposed arrangement or pulls back from *the proposal as such*. It costs almost nothing because a proposal is being floated anyway, and it separates the readings in a way neither the account's recurrence test nor the objection's alternatives do. I would actively look for it.

**What I would actually do.** Not a household settlement meeting, and not the rival's "what is this flat" question as an opener either. The rival's own r9 names the risk and r6 does not mitigate it: asking two flatmates separately what the household is can read as an inquiry into loyalty or commitment, and can produce the very withdrawal it is meant to diagnose.

Instead: one concrete recurring item, floated as a two-week trial rather than a rule, with three things observed — (a) does it recur, (b) how does each flatmate react to the proposal itself, (c) does complaint migrate. That single move is practical relief and a probe under all three readings. Pair the separate approach to the withdrawing flatmate not with a request to settle terms but with something in that person's interest — an owned zone, or a rotation with a default outcome nobody has to negotiate in the moment (r8). That converts the approach from a summons into an offer, which answers r9 at the level of the action instead of the caveat. Hold the lease and living-arrangement question as a *named* endpoint if the probes fail (account step 5, rival r11); name it when it arrives rather than drifting into it.

**Left open, and one thing none of the three raises.** I decline to adopt rival r3 unconditionally. I leave open: r2; whether load imbalance is present; whether the avoidance is about form, content, load, or something outside chores; and every specific — the actual chores, how long this has run, what the withdrawing friend has said.

None of the three notices that all of them address the flatmate who posed the problem and propose further initiatives from that quarter. If any part of the trouble is a legitimacy question — who gets to set terms — then more initiatives from the same party is not a neutral remedy; it may be part of the pattern. That is not a reason to do nothing. It is a reason to make at least one move an offer that can be declined without penalty rather than a proposal that demands a response.

Finally, reference hygiene. The objection's o3 cites "p.objection.0#c3," and no such record exists in the objection's exposed set (c1 and c2 only). The rival's r1 cites body hash e3647350a300c0ed, which is not the account hash exposed here.
